findings.text: Directory creation through the filesystem mkdir hook validates the requested name, verifies that the parent is live, enforces ancestor depth and descendant limits, allocates and links a child object, populates its control entries, enables controllers, and activates the node; failures during population or control enabling trigger synchronous destruction before releasing the parent lock. A name containing a line break is rejected to preserve parsability of process membership listings.

Directory removal resolves the target only when still live and otherwise reports success without action. Removal fails while any task remains attached or any child remains online, since dead children linger on the sibling list and cannot be judged by list emptiness. Successful removal marks the object and its set links dead, terminates associated states, clears and removes the directory node, adjusts ancestor live and dying counts with frozen accounting, issues lifetime notifications, and drops the base reference, finishing states that were never populated.

Child allocation reserves a flexible ancestor table sized by depth, initializes reference counting with a deferred release callback, creates the directory node with caller filesystem credentials, and establishes parent linkage, hierarchy root, and depth. Housekeeping, statistics, and pressure tracking are initialized with ordered unwinding on failure. Ancestor pointers, effective freeze state, release notification, and cloning flags are inherited; a frozen parent causes the child to start frozen with a timestamp. Lifetime online notification precedes commitment of ancestor descendant counts, sibling linkage, hierarchy population count, parent liveness hold, and control propagation, with default hierarchy children starting without automatic control inheritance.

Objects on the default hierarchy can be resolved from a persistent filesystem identifier. Path formatting fills a caller buffer when the node exists and silently does nothing otherwise. Reference acquisition requires a directory node and a live object obtained under read side protection, failing when absent or already dead. Namespace aware resolution additionally requires descent from the caller current default hierarchy root and drops the reference on mismatch.

Process membership reporting iterates all hierarchies under combined read side and interrupt disabled spin protection, skipping the default hierarchy when hidden and skipping unmounted roots. Each line records hierarchy identifier, attached legacy controller names, optional hierarchy name, and the member path within the reader namespace, translating an oversize path result into a name too long failure. Traditional hierarchies report exiting tasks at the root, while default hierarchy zombies retain their prior path with a deletion marker when the object is already dead.

A file handle can be resolved to its owning object by interpreting the directory entry filesystem type and directory nature, then dereferencing the node backpointer under read side protection and acquiring an online reference on the requested controller state or the owning object itself. Handles outside control filesystems, non directory nodes, missing backpointers, or states that are not online yield failures. A default hierarchy only variant rejects objects from other hierarchies after dropping the acquired reference.

Early boot establishes the default root, marks its self state as reference exempt, binds the initial task to the initial set, assigns each subsystem its index and names with fallback legacy naming, validates allocation callbacks and name lengths, rejects statistics use with early subsystems, and initializes only early subsystems. Subsystem initialization creates the root state, links it, disables reference counting for roots, assigns a fixed identifier during early phase, records the state in the initial set, accumulates fork exit release and can fork callback presence, asserts no tasks have been created yet, and brings the root state online.

Late boot verifies the subsystem count fits a fixed width mask, registers base control files, initializes global statistics locking, holds the initial namespace, prepares deferred reaping structures, hashes the initial set, initializes lifetime notification for filtering, and sets up the default root. Each subsystem then receives a persistent identifier or full initialization, linkage into default root membership, mask updates for enabled implicit inhibited and threaded controllers with validation of threading for implicit ones, control file registration distinguishing shared versus split default and legacy tables, optional binding, and directory population, followed by rehashing, creation of mount and filesystem registrations, a statistics proc entry with optional cpuset support, and namespace tree insertion.

Three single active ordered workqueues serve offline release and free phases. Per processor dead task lists and lazy interrupt work are prepared where supported and omitted otherwise. Statistics initialization allocates per processor update lists when a subsystem is given and always initializes locking and per processor heads.

The global hierarchy mutex serializes offline transition, hierarchy limit checks, destruction, killed state draining, finish handling, and release processing. Offline and destroy paths assert the mutex is held. Work handlers acquire it around the critical section and release before dropping references. A state cannot disappear while the mutex is held during parent chain draining.

A dedicated interrupt disabled spin lock guards ancestor descendant counts, dying descendant counts, frozen descendant counts, set link liveness, and membership reporting consistency. Creation commits counts, destruction transfers live counts to dying with frozen adjustment, release decrements dying chain counts for non self states and dying descendant chain counts for self states, and membership display holds both read side protection and the spin lock. The directory node backpointer is cleared and read under read side rules so control paths that bypass the filesystem remain safe against concurrent removal.

Controller state shutdown proceeds in ordered phases. Reference teardown decrements an online counter and schedules deferred work only on last put. The offline worker walks toward the root while each parent reaches zero, invoking optional offline callbacks, clearing the online flag, detaching the hierarchy slot, waking offline waiters, and dropping references. Final release is deferred to a dedicated queue, marks released, detaches from siblings, flushes statistics, and diverges: non self states release identifiers, invoke release callbacks, and decrement dying subsystem counters along ancestors with an expectation of no descendants, while self states emit release tracing, flush root statistics, decrement dying descendant chains, and null the node backpointer, before scheduling freed work. A separate finish worker serializes completion and reference drop.

Group lifetime moves from allocation through commitment to destruction and deferred freeing. Allocation and notification precede atomic commitment of counts and linkage. Directory creation adds population, control enabling, tracing, and activation, unwinding through locked destruction on late failure while holding an extra node reference until freeing. Destruction requires quiescence of tasks and online children, then disables further binding, terminates states synchronously, removes the directory, updates ancestor accounting, notifies offline, kills the base reference, and completes unpopulated states immediately.

Ancestor live counts increase only at commitment and decrease only at destruction, with a matching increase in dying counts; frozen descendant counts track frozen membership symmetrically. Non self release expects zero descendants while tolerating nonzero dying subsystem totals due to repeated activation cycles. Creation is refused when any ancestor would exceed its descendant or depth ceiling.

Root states are never destroyed and carry a no reference flag. Early root identifiers use identifier one with identifier zero reserved for the root group itself, later replaced by persistent allocator values. Initial task membership starts in the initial set, and creation records a monotonically increasing serial number for each new self state.

The group object carries hierarchy root linkage, depth level, ancestor table, directory node pointer, housekeeping state, self controller state with parent sibling children linkage reference count flags serial number and online counter, descendant and dying descendant totals with per subsystem dying arrays and ceilings for depth and breadth, control masks for subtree and enabled state, release and cloning flags, freezer effective and timing state with frozen descendant totals, offline wait queue, set link list, threaded child count, and subsystem slots. Controller state carries subsystem backpointer, owning group pointer, identifier, descendant count, and deferred work items for kill finish release and freed phases.

Checking sibling list emptiness is unsafe for removal decisions because dead children remain linked during draining; only online child status is reliable. Directory resolution without liveness locking can observe nodes being removed, so backpointer access must use read side dereference. Accepting control characters in names would corrupt line oriented membership output and is therefore refused. An extra node hold guarantees directory accessibility until deferred freeing completes.

The implementation enforces a maximum of thirty two controller subsystems. Name validation, missing live parents, hierarchy ceiling exceeded, allocation failure, busy removal due to tasks or online children, non directory or unknown identifier lookup, cross namespace escape, non control filesystem or offline state resolution, and oversize path rendering each produce distinct failure outcomes recognized by callers, including invalid argument, no device, resource unavailable, out of memory, busy, no entry, bad descriptor, and oversize translated to name too long.

Task creation initializes the child membership pointer to the global initial set and prepares its membership list node. Filesystem operations dispatch directory creation and removal to dedicated handlers alongside option display and path formatting.
